claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has been produced in a hierarchical-heterostructured state featuring multilevel chemical fluctuations.
A physics-informed reduced-order ML model can integrate hierarchical microstructural descriptors with thermophysical parameters.
The proposed model can predict Young's modulus in hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed model can predict yield strength in hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed model can predict fracture toughness in hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
Replacing full-scale atomistic calculations with a reduced-order surrogate will lower computational cost.
Phase fraction, characteristic length scales, and interphase-boundary descriptors can be used as model inputs for the target mechanical properties.
Grain-size distribution, phase connectivity, and hierarchical composition fluctuations mediate the relationship between internal structure and macroscopic deformation and fracture.
The incorporated microstructural features govern dislocation mobility.
The incorporated microstructural features govern crack propagation.
Chemical fluctuations and hierarchical phase connectivity influence elastic, plastic, and fracture behavior.
The surrogate will reduce prediction-error margins by at least 50% relative to conventional atomistic or CALPHAD-based methods.
The surrogate will reduce computational costs by approximately 80%.
Full first-principles and high-fidelity computational methods can require large computational resources.
Existing first-principles, CALPHAD, and high-fidelity methods struggle to predict fracture toughness in heterogeneous HfNbTiVAl10.
The model is intended to apply at room temperature, under quasi-static tensile and fracture conditions, and only to microstructures within the training domain.
The model will lose reliability for out-of-distribution phase fractions, grain sizes, chemical fluctuations, temperatures, or strain rates.
Toughening mechanisms such as mesoscopic crack deflection may not be captured if the selected descriptors omit deformation-initiating features.
The hypothesis is to be falsified if at least 70% of blinded samples have predictions deviating by more than ±15% for one or more target properties.
